tagline: From Nancy’s battlefield cemetery through rolling fields to the ferry landing
intro: The Zollicoffer-Thomas Scenic Byway runs 10.36 miles from Nancy to the ferry landing, through the Mill Springs battlefield landscape. The National Park Service describes rolling fields where an early Union victory revealed Kentucky’s strategic importance to both sides. Kentucky designated the scenic route in September 2001.

On January 19, 1862, Confederate troops attacked George H. Thomas’s Union force at Logan’s Crossroads. Felix Zollicoffer was killed, and Union counterattacks forced the Confederates from the field. Preservation later combined land purchases with the acquisition of development rights in the rural battlefield landscape. Congress authorized a national monument in 2019; after acquiring property, the National Park Service established the unit in September 2020. The battlefield extends across both sides of what is now Lake Cumberland, with Confederate fortification areas near Mill Springs and Beech Grove as well as the main battlefield.

Start at Nancy, where the national cemetery stands beside the battlefield museum. From KY 80, follow KY 235 and Old Mill Springs Battlefield Road to the road’s end at Ferry Landing, Tour Stop 8. The town of Mill Springs lies across Lake Cumberland, requiring a separate drive by Highways 90 and 1275 to reach the south-side sites.

moments.title: Mill Springs National Cemetery
moments.text: The cemetery began with soldiers buried in large trenches after the Battle of Mill Springs. Initially called Logan’s Cross Roads Cemetery, it became a national cemetery after the Civil War and received remains transferred from other battlefield cemeteries in the region. William H. Logan donated additional land in 1867; he and his wife were later buried here. The adjacent battlefield museum overlooks the ground where Union forces camped. Administered by the Department of Veterans Affairs, the cemetery continues to receive burials. Its role extends beyond the men killed in the 1862 battle.

moments.title: Mill Springs battlefield
moments.text: A marked stump identifies the former Zollie Tree, associated with the place where Felix Zollicoffer fell. Lightning destroyed the tree. Zollicoffer wore a conspicuous white raincoat. During the battle, Zollicoffer approached the Union 4th Kentucky Infantry, mistaking them for Confederates firing on their own men, and was killed. Zollicoffer Park also contains a Confederate mass grave; nearby markers represent soldiers thought or confirmed to be buried in it. The Union dead were buried at the national cemetery in Nancy, while the Confederate burials remained on the battlefield at Zollicoffer Park.

moments.title: Mill Springs Mill
moments.text: Mill Springs Mill’s 40-foot wheel is larger than the one installed when the building went up in 1877. The original wooden wheel measured 28 feet; the larger replacement arrived when the mill was sold in 1907. The three-story frame building rests on large stone columns, on a descent toward the Cumberland River. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers restored the mill at Mill Springs in 1976. The wheel measures three feet across. The site’s National Register documentation recognized both its unusual wheel and the mill’s role in local commercial trade.
